newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-DEVERS WINS BATTLE OF OLYMPIC MEDALISTS AT INDOOR MEET.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-DEVERS WINS BATTLE OF OLYMPIC MEDALISTS AT INDOOR MEET.

text.p: Gail Devers overcame injury to post the year's third fastest 60-meters time and win a battle of Olympic medalists Saturday at the Mobil Invitational grand prix meet.

Devers, the 1992 and 1996 Olympic champion in the 100 meters, was clocked at 7.07 seconds to beat Gwen Torrence, the 1992 Olympic gold medalist at 200 meters, and fellow-American Olympian Carlette Guidry.
Torrence ran 7.12, her best of the season, and Guidry, who came back to win the 200 meters, was third in 7.14.
Another Atlanta Olympic champion, Allen Johnson, won the 60 meter hurdles here for the third consecutive year.

Other winners on the day included Jamaica's Michael Green in the men's 60 meters (6.53), Jackeline Maranga of Kenya in the women's mile (handtimed in 4:30.3) and Julius Achon of Uganda in the men's mile.

Achon, who runs for George Mason University, which hosts the meet, covered the mile in 3:57.41, edging Zimbabwe's Passmore Furusa (3:57.82). Ireland's Niall Bruton was a disappointing eighth (4:09.44). American Jason Pyrah, second at the Millrose Games two weeks ago, was third in 3:59.09.
The Devers-Torrence competition was the highlight of the meet, especially since it almost did not come off.

"I'm very pleased, more so because I didn't leave the meet on a stretcher," said Devers, who has been bothered by a right hamstring injury she suffered last month in Germany. Despite the injury, she posted a time bettered this year by only Irina Privalova of Russia and Nigeria's Christy Opara (both 7.02).

"I came in iffy. If I felt anything in my warmup, I wasn't supposed to run, but I didn't feel anything then or during the race," said Devers, hopeful she will be fit enough to run in next weekend's U.S. indoor nationals in Atlanta.

Torrence is also pointing for the Atlanta meet, though she won't go on to the world championships. "I'm not ready. Until I can run in 7-flat, I won't be. And I'm not that gung ho this year," said Torrence.
Johnson's time, 7.57, was the slowest of his three victories here. "I wasn't disappointed. This is only my third meet of the year. Usually I've run 15 by now," Johnson said.
"I'm using this to prepare for outdoors. I want to win next week and the worlds, but everything I'm doing now is to benefit my outdoor season."

Two-time U.S. Olympian Steve Scott set an American record in the Masters Mile. The 40-year-old Scott, who had cancer surgery in 1994, went the last quarter in 59.87 to clock 4.14.27. The previous mark, 4:14.41, was held by Ken Popejoy. Ireland's Eamonn Coughlan has the world Masters mark, 3:58.15.
